title: Arc Length: a Sum of Tiny Hypotenuses

steps.body:
How long is a curve? Cut it into tiny straight pieces and add them up — the oldest trick in the book, and it works here too.

One tiny piece moves dx across and dy up, so by **Pythagoras** its length is √(dx² + dy²). Factor out dt:

**L = ∫ √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt**

Every arc length is a Riemann sum of tiny hypotenuses.
A straight line, to check the formula.
explanationVariants: dx/dt = 3 and dy/dt = 4, so the integrand is √(9 + 16) = 5, a constant. Over t from 0 to 1 that gives L = 5.
And the 3-4-5 triangle confirms it: the point travels from (0,0) to (3,4), a distance of 5. The formula reproduces the geometry.

widget.prompt: x = 3t, y = 4t, for t from 0 to 1. Find the arc length.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 3 + 4 — adding the legs rather than taking the hypotenuse. Pythagoras gives √(9 + 16) = 5.
That is 3² + 4². The length is the SQUARE ROOT of that: 5.
That is the range of t. The distance travelled is 5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: √(3² + 4²) = 5, and the point really does travel from (0,0) to (3,4).

steps.body: Why it is Pythagoras all the way down.

widget.prompt: Cut the curve into straight pieces.

panels.title: Straighten a tiny piece
panels.body: Zoom far enough into a differentiable curve and it becomes a straight line — that is the local straightness from C2. So a tiny piece of arc IS a tiny straight segment.

panels.title: Measure it with Pythagoras
panels.body: That segment moves dx across and dy up, so its length is √(dx² + dy²). Nothing new is happening: it is the distance formula, applied to something very small.

panels.title: Add them up
panels.body: Sum the pieces and let them shrink, and you have an integral. Arc length is the one place where 'the integral is a sum' is not a metaphor — you are literally adding up lengths.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the first panel is why cutting the curve is legal at all.
widget.successFeedback: Local straightness makes each piece a hypotenuse. The integral just adds them up.

explanationVariants: x = cos t, y = sin t gives dx/dt = −sin t and dy/dt = cos t, so the integrand is √(sin² + cos²) = 1. Over t from 0 to π/2 the length is π/2 ≈ 1.571.
A quarter of the unit circle's circumference 2π is π/2 — the formula and the geometry agree exactly.

widget.prompt: x = cos t, y = sin t, for t from 0 to π/2. Find the arc length, to three decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the WHOLE circumference, 2π. You travelled only a quarter of the way round.
That is the integrand — which is 1 everywhere, because the point moves at unit speed. The LENGTH is that integrated over π/2.
That is π/4. The sweep runs from 0 to π/2, so the length is π/2 ≈ 1.571.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The integrand is √(sin² + cos²) = 1, so L = π/2 ≈ 1.571 — a quarter of the circumference.

steps.body:
The speed is the integrand.

√((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) is exactly the **speed** of the point tracing the curve — the magnitude of its velocity vector.

So arc length is **∫ speed dt**, which is the total distance travelled. That is the same sentence as C5's ∫|v| dt, one dimension up.

explanationVariants: The integrand IS the speed — the magnitude of the velocity vector ⟨dx/dt, dy/dt⟩. Integrating a speed gives a distance, which is exactly what arc length is.
It is the C5 idea (∫|v| dt is the total distance) in two dimensions, where |v| is now a Pythagorean magnitude.

options.label: The SPEED of the point — the magnitude of its velocity vector.
options.feedback: Right, and so arc length is ∫ speed dt: the total distance travelled. It is C5's ∫|v| dt, one dimension up.

options.label: The SLOPE of the curve — the ratio of the two rates of change.
options.feedback: The slope is the RATIO of the two rates. This is their Pythagorean combination, which is a magnitude, not a direction.

options.label: The ACCELERATION of the point — how quickly its velocity changes.
options.feedback: Acceleration needs SECOND derivatives. These are first derivatives, so this is a velocity magnitude.

options.label: The AREA under the curve — the integral of y with respect to x.
options.feedback: Every term inside that root is a LENGTH per unit time, so the whole expression is a speed. An area would need a length times a length, and there is none here.

hints: dx/dt = 8 and dy/dt = 15, both constant — that fixes the speed.
Speed = √(64 + 225) = 17, constant for the whole journey.
Distance = speed × time, so solve 51 = 17t for t.
explanationVariants: The constant speed is √(8² + 15²) = 17. Distance = speed × time, so 51 = 17t gives t = 3.
Same relationship as before, run in reverse: instead of time → distance, this asks distance → time.

widget.prompt: A point moves with x = 8t, y = 15t. It travels 51 units of arc length. What value of t does that take?

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplies distance by speed instead of dividing — solve 51 = 17t for t: t = 51/17 = 3.
That divides by only the x-rate, 8. The actual speed combines both rates: √(8² + 15²) = 17, so t = 51/17 = 3.
That divides by only the y-rate, 15. The actual speed combines both rates: √(8² + 15²) = 17, so t = 3.

takeaways: L = ∫√((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt — every tiny piece of arc is a hypotenuse, and the integral adds them up.
The integrand is the SPEED, so arc length is ∫ speed dt: the total distance travelled.
It is C5's ∫|v| dt in two dimensions, where the magnitude is now Pythagorean.

concept.body: Each tiny piece of the curve is a right triangle: dx across, dy up, and the piece of arc as the hypotenuse. Its length is √(dx² + dy²). Add up the hypotenuses and you have the length of the curve.

widget.prompt: A tiny piece of curve moves 5 across and 12 up. How long is it?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 5 + 12 — adding the legs. The piece of arc is the HYPOTENUSE: √(25 + 144) = 13.
That is 5² + 12². Take the square root: 13.
